posts.body:
Meta just titled an update "You don't beat the auction, you brief it."

That one line changes what "optimising a campaign" even means.

Most people treat the auction like a machine to outsmart — tighter targeting, clever bidding, a sharper audience. Meta is saying the opposite. The auction is not solved, it is briefed. You tell it what a real outcome looks like, and it goes and finds more of that.

The brief isn't your copy or your creative. It's the signal you feed back in — the actual purchases, the actual qualified leads, sent into the ad account so the system learns what to chase.

Across nine Meta ad accounts I've run, 7,341 lead-form submissions came in. Every one of those sits in Meta's own lead centre, tagged to the exact ad and form that produced it. That log is the brief. Most accounts never check it, so the auction keeps chasing whatever it chased on day one.

Open your Ads Manager today. Look at your lead form's questions. Are you telling Meta which of those leads turned into actual sales, or is it still guessing from the form alone?

posts.hook: Meta just published how agencies are testing incrementality. Incrementality means asking: did the ad cause the sale, or would that person have bought anyway?
posts.body:
Meta just published how agencies are testing incrementality.

Incrementality means asking: did the ad cause the sale, or would that person have bought anyway?

Most small advertisers never check this. They look at "results" in Ads Manager and assume every one came from the ad. Meta's own post admits that is not always true, and shows agencies running holdout tests to find out — showing the ad to one group and not another, then comparing what each group actually bought.

You don't need an agency's budget to borrow the idea. Pick your best-spending campaign. Pause it for a few days in a market or audience segment you can isolate, and watch if sales actually drop, or barely move.

If sales barely move, that budget wasn't creating buyers. It was catching people who were going to buy anyway, and the ad got the credit.

This is the same discipline behind every number I publish — cost per lead means amount spent divided by leads counted in Meta's own lead centre, nothing modelled. Incrementality testing is that same honesty, aimed at the sale itself.

Have you ever turned a campaign off on purpose, just to see what happens to sales without it?

Nine Meta ad accounts. One order, every time, before touching a single ad.

Most people fixing a slow account start with the creative — new image, new headline, new offer. That's usually step six, not step one.

Before any of that, there's a fixed order: check what the campaign is actually optimised to do, check what the ad set calls success, check where the lead actually lands, check who looks at it and when. Only after all of that is cleared does the creative get touched.

Across 7,341 lead-form submissions on nine accounts, the leak was almost never the ad itself. It was somewhere upstream or downstream of it — a setting nobody opened in months, or a lead nobody followed up within the hour.

The order matters because fixing creative on a broken foundation just gets you a prettier version of the same leak.

Changing the ad first just makes the real leak harder to find.
Start in Ads Manager, not the ad. Open your campaign and find the Performance goal line first.

Fix the account in this order: goal, ad set, form, follow-up. Creative comes last, not first.

posts.body:
Google just published a holiday shopping guide built on search data, not guesses.

Most small businesses read that as "big brand news" and move on. The distinction that matters: it's not about ad budgets, it's about timing — when people start searching before they buy.

Here's the mechanic worth knowing. Google tracks search interest by category and publishes when it peaks, weeks before the actual buying date. If you sell anything seasonal, that peak is when your ad or your Google Business Profile needs to already be live, not when you finally get around to it.

Most small accounts do the opposite. They start campaigns the week they feel ready, not the week their customer starts looking. By the time the ad goes live, the searcher has already bought from whoever showed up first.

This costs nothing to check. Go to Google Trends, type your product category, and look at the last two years. The search spike repeats on roughly the same week every year.

What week does your category's search interest actually spike, and is your account live before it or during it?

One line in a lead form decides whether your sales team talks to buyers, or to browsers.

Most forms ask for name, phone, email. That tells you nothing about whether the person can actually buy what you sell.

A Tirupur apparel manufacturer ran a campaign where the ad and the form both stated a 200-piece minimum order, up front. 19 wholesale buyers responded, at under $6 an enquiry.

Compare that to the same manufacturer's wider lead campaigns: 4,248 leads at ₹16.58 each across six campaigns. Cheaper leads, no qualifying question in front of them.

Neither number is wrong. They are two different products. Cheap leads fill a sheet. Qualified leads fill a sales call.

The qualifying question is not about your product. It is about the one thing that would make someone unable to buy from you at all — minimum order size, budget, location, timeline. Put that one thing in the form, in plain words, before you ask for a phone number.

You will get fewer leads. You will also stop handing your sales team people who were never going to say yes.

posts.body:
Pollo AI just announced it turns creative ideas into ad campaigns using OpenAI's models. "Pollo AI turns creative ideas into campaigns with OpenAI."

Writing an ad is not the same as finding out who it reaches.

Any tool that writes campaign copy is solving the easy half. It can give you five headlines in ten seconds. It cannot tell you if the 200 people who filled your form actually have the budget your product needs — nobody can, until they respond and you talk to them.

Across our nine Meta ad accounts, 7,341 people filled a lead form. Cost per lead is just amount spent divided by leads, pulled straight from Ads Manager. That number is easy. What happens after someone submits the form is the part no AI writes for you.

Say a clinic uses a tool like this to generate twenty ad variations by lunch. The variations are not the bottleneck. Whether the front desk calls lead number fourteen before it goes cold is the bottleneck, and that has nothing to do with GPT-6.1 Sol or any model behind it.

So before trying a tool like this, check one thing in your own account: Ads Manager → your campaign → the ad set → Performance goal. What is it actually optimising for right now, leads or something else?

posts.body:
OpenAI published "Helping teens learn, plan, and shape the future of AI" this week.

Most posts will stop at "OpenAI builds teen safety tools." That's the headline, not the point.

The point is simpler: a generation is about to grow up treating AI as the default way to ask a question, not a novelty. That changes what a search, a form fill or an enquiry even looks like in a few years.

If you run ads today, nothing in your account needs to change tomorrow because of this. But the people filling your lead forms five years from now learned to ask AI before they learned to Google. Your form, your landing page, your follow-up message — all built for people who type keywords. The next buyer might just ask an assistant to find and compare for them.

Nobody can tell you exactly what that means for cost per lead yet. Anyone who says they can is guessing. What you can do today is keep your own numbers honest, so when the shift shows up in your account, you notice it in your data and not in a feeling.

slides.text: One OpenAI update this week has nothing to do with chatbots.
Everyone is reading it as a safety story. That is the smaller part.
OpenAI's 7 October post is about teaching teenagers to use AI as a daily tool, not a toy.
That means the people who will fill your lead forms in five years are learning AI first, search second.
Today a buyer types your product name into Google. Soon they may just ask an assistant to find it.
Your landing page, your ad copy, your form — all built for someone typing keywords by hand.
Nobody knows yet what an AI-first buyer does to cost per lead or conversion rate.
But you can check one thing this week: how many of your form leads come from someone clearly reading, not just tapping through.
Open your lead form questions. Count how many need a real answer versus a pre-filled tap.
That ratio is your form's readiness for a buyer who thinks before they click, not just one who scrolls fast.
This change won't hit your ad account tomorrow. It will hit whoever didn't check their form today.

posts.hook: GPT-6 landed this week. "Intelligent UI" builds the screen for your question, not the other way round. Most posts will stop at that headline. Here's what it means if you run your own ads.
posts.body:
GPT-6 landed this week. "Intelligent UI" builds the screen for your question, not the other way round.

Most posts will stop at that headline. Here's what it means if you run your own ads.

An interface that writes itself still needs you to know what you're asking for. Ask ChatGPT to "check my Meta campaign" and it can read a screenshot. It cannot open Ads Manager, click into your ad set, and tell you your Performance goal is set to Conversations when you meant Purchases.

That gap is where cost per lead actually gets decided. Not in the chat window — inside the account, in a setting most people never open.

Smarter tools change what you can ask. They don't change what you need to know to ask it well. A founder who can't read a lifetime view in Ads Manager will get a very fluent wrong answer, faster than before.

Across nine of our own ad accounts, every lead is still counted the same way it always was: a submission in Meta's lead centre, tied to the ad and form that produced it. No model, no estimate.

If you want a second set of eyes on how your account is actually set up, before you hand the thinking to a chatbot, that's something we do for free on jothiswaroop.com.
